opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the backgrounds are more varied than people tend to assume. The common thread isn't a particular degree. It's strong software engineering combined with real curiosity about the alignment problem itself.

The most obvious fit is someone who has worked with machine learning at scale: training large models, debugging distributed training runs, building evaluation infrastructure, or doing reinforcement learning work. A lot of what we do is empirical. We fine-tune models, run experiments on things like reward modeling or scalable oversight, and try to measure whether a technique actually helps. So people who can move quickly in a big ML codebase and keep experiments clean and reproducible are extremely valuable.

But I'd stress that you don't need to have been an ML researcher already. Some of the strongest research engineers I've worked with came from general software engineering, from places like startups or big tech infrastructure teams. They were excellent programmers, they picked up the ML side fairly quickly, and they brought a level of engineering discipline that research teams often lack. If you've built reliable systems, can read and write a lot of code fast, and are comfortable debugging things when you don't know where the problem is, that transfers really well.

People from physics, math, or other quantitative sciences also often do well, especially if they've done a lot of computational work. They tend to be good at thinking carefully about what an experiment actually shows.

Beyond the technical background, a few traits really matter. One is caring about the problem. Alignment research can be frustrating and ambiguous, and it helps a lot if you're motivated by wanting it to go well. Another is good research taste, or at least the willingness to develop it: asking "is this the right experiment?" rather than just executing a task. And a third is being collaborative and low-ego, because so much of the work happens in tight loops between researchers and engineers, and honestly the line between those roles is pretty blurry on our team.

So if someone listening is a strong engineer who's been reading about alignment and thinking "I'm not an ML PhD, so this isn't for me," I'd really encourage them to reconsider. Get some hands-on experience: reimplement a few papers, train some small models, play with RL from human feedback. That's often enough to be a competitive candidate.

r001.rationale: It recommends reimplementing papers as hands-on preparation, alongside training small models and trying RL from human feedback; it also says people from quantitative sciences can do well.

r002.rationale: It says prior ML research experience is not required, but does not state that most hires have not previously worked on alignment.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes strong software engineering as the common thread and describes ML experience as one promising background, not as the core expertise.

r004.rationale: It says some engineers picked up the ML side quickly, but does not state that alignment knowledge can be learned after joining.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's broader than people expect. The thing I'm really looking for in a research engineer is someone who can take a vague research idea and turn it into a working experiment quickly, and then iterate on it. That's the core loop. And there are a lot of paths that lead to being good at that.

The most obvious one is people coming from a strong software engineering background who've then picked up machine learning, either on the job or through self-study. Those folks tend to be really valuable because the bottleneck on a lot of alignment research isn't having clever ideas, it's actually running the experiments at scale without everything falling over. If you've spent a few years shipping production systems, writing code that other people can read and build on, debugging distributed training jobs, that transfers extremely well. We care a lot about engineering rigor.

Then there's the more classic ML route: people who've done a PhD or a master's, or just a lot of hands-on ML work, and who are comfortable with training models, understanding what's going on inside them, reading papers and reimplementing things. For that group, the question I usually ask is whether they've actually built things end to end, rather than only run someone else's pipeline. Have you trained a language model from scratch? Have you gotten an RL setup to work? Those are surprisingly discriminating.

But I'd also say we've hired people who didn't fit either of those neatly. People who came from physics or math, or from a quantitative role somewhere else entirely, who taught themselves and then did some impressive independent project. What matters is less the credential and more whether you can demonstrate that you've done serious work. A GitHub repo where you reproduced a result, or a write-up where you tried something and explained what you learned, honestly counts for a lot.

And then on top of the technical side there's a set of things that are harder to screen for but really matter. Do you actually care about the problem? Alignment is still a pretty young field, and a lot of the work is messy and underspecified. You need to be comfortable with that, comfortable asking "wait, does this experiment even test what we think it tests?" and pushing back when it doesn't. The best research engineers I've worked with are the ones who gradually start generating their own research directions, so the line between engineer and researcher blurs over time.

So if someone's listening and thinking "I'm not sure I'm qualified," I'd say: if you can write good code, you understand modern deep learning well enough to implement and debug it, and you're genuinely motivated by the problem, you should probably apply. We're often more flexible than people assume, and we'd rather see the application than not.

r001.rationale: The response mentions people from physics, math, or quantitative roles doing independent projects, and separately mentions reimplementing ML work. It does not clearly identify reimplementing existing papers as a preparation route for people transitioning from STEM fields.

r002.rationale: The response does not state whether most hires have prior alignment experience.

r003.rationale: The response presents understanding modern deep learning well enough to implement and debug it as a key qualification, alongside strong coding and engineering skills.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that alignment knowledge can be learned after joining the team.

astra-6.text:
There are a few different backgrounds that can be really useful. One is having experience with machine learning — actually training models, debugging them, and understanding why an experiment isn’t working. But I’m also excited about people who are very strong software engineers, even if they haven’t done much machine learning yet. A lot of the work involves building reliable infrastructure and making it easy to run experiments and understand the results.

The research side matters too: being curious, being able to turn a vague question into an experiment, and being willing to change your mind when the results don’t match your intuition. You don’t necessarily need a PhD for that.

And then I’d want someone who is motivated by alignment and wants to think carefully about whether the thing we’re building actually helps us make progress on it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions training and debugging models, but does not identify reimplementing existing machine learning papers as a preparation route.

r002.rationale: It does not state whether most people Jan Leike’s team hires have prior alignment experience.

r003.rationale: It presents machine learning experience as one useful background, while also welcoming strong software engineers without much machine learning experience; it does not identify machine learning as the core expertise.

r004.rationale: It does not say that the alignment knowledge needed for the role can be learned after joining.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different backgrounds that can work well. One is having a lot of experience with machine learning: you’ve trained models, you know how to run experiments, and you’re good at figuring out why something isn’t working.

But we’re also interested in people who are strong software engineers and don’t necessarily have much machine learning experience yet. There’s a lot of engineering involved in making experiments run reliably, building infrastructure, and helping researchers iterate quickly. You can learn a lot of the machine learning on the job.

And then another useful background is security — being good at finding ways systems can fail, questioning assumptions, and thinking adversarially. That seems particularly relevant for alignment.

Across those backgrounds, I’d look for people who are curious, can work independently on an ambiguous problem, and really want to understand whether the thing they’re building actually does what they intended.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention reimplementing machine learning papers or describe it as preparation for a STEM-to-alignment transition.

r002.rationale: It says some strong software engineers may have little machine learning experience, but does not state that most hires lack prior alignment experience.

r003.rationale: Machine learning experience is presented as one of several useful backgrounds, not as the core expertise needed for the role.

r004.rationale: The response says machine learning can be learned on the job; it does not say alignment knowledge can be learned after joining.
